note_sections.t: Ongoing assessment after a previous low-grade prostate cancer diagnosis alongside persistent PSA elevation.

First investigated for an incidental PSA rise in mid-2022, this 64-year-old gentleman carries a diagnosis of low-grade prostate cancer. A retired plumber, he shares a household with his wife and stays physically active through regular cycling, logging roughly 30 kilometres per session on 3 occasions weekly. Urinary complaints are negligible, yielding an IPSS score of 1; he denies hematuria or pelvic discomfort. His medical background includes well-managed hypertension and hypercholesterolaemia, treated with amlodipine, metoprolol, atorvastatin, and rosuvastatin, with a cardiology check-up completed 6 months ago. Alcohol consumption averages 13 units each week, and he reports no significant lifestyle shifts or new systemic complaints. Administrative needs include large-print correspondence to accommodate mild visual impairment, while his adult son acts as the designated primary contact. Non-smoker status is documented.

DRE — texture: smooth and firm; mobility: unremarkable; asymmetry: absent. The prostate appears symmetrically enlarged without discrete nodules. Systemic assessment shows normal findings overall. Blood pressure registers at 160/86 mmHg, accompanied by a steady pulse of 74 beats per minute. Palpation of the abdomen uncovers no masses or organ enlargement, and peripheral lymphadenopathy is absent.
